title: Debugging
summary: Finding off-by-one slips, shared-state mutation, async ordering mistakes and failures that travel through several functions.

concepts.title: Bugs from shared and mutated state
Following a failure through several functions

misconceptions.description: Believes reading one index past the end adds or does nothing instead of producing undefined.
Believes reading an array index that does not exist throws an error.
Believes the end argument of slice is included in the result, or that it counts items.
Believes spread or Object.assign copies nested arrays and objects too.
Believes sort, reverse or splice return an independent copy while leaving the original alone.
Believes map never changes the original items, even when the callback edits the objects it receives.
Believes calling an async function delays its entire body until the caller finishes.
Believes an async function runs to the end before the caller continues, ignoring await.
Believes await makes other calls of the same function wait for it.
Believes code after a throw, or later steps of a rejected chain, keep running normally.
Believes finally does not run when an error is passing through to a caller.
Believes a promise chain stays rejected after a catch has handled it.
Believes the value a catch handler returns is discarded, so the next step receives undefined.
Believes a start index is fixed by adding or taking away one after multiplying, instead of counting the whole pages before the page.
Believes a spread copy shares every property with the original, so changing any property of the copy changes the original.
Believes returning the async call, or scheduling it with a timer, makes the lines after it wait for it.

conceptCard.title: Boundaries and off-by-one errors
conceptCard.body: An array with n items has indexes 0 to n - 1. A loop that keeps going while i <= n reads one slot too many, and one that stops early at i < n - 1 skips the last item. slice(start, end) includes start and excludes end. A negative start counts from the end.

lessons.title: Bugs from shared and mutated state

conceptCard.title: Bugs from shared and mutated state
conceptCard.body: Arrays and objects are shared by reference. A second name, a method that works in place, or a shallow copy can all point at the same data, so a change through one name shows up in the others. Copy the level you change.

conceptCard.title: Bugs from asynchronous ordering
conceptCard.body: An async function runs normally until its first await, and the rest continues later. A value read before an await can be stale after it. Two async calls take turns: after each await, a call goes to the back of the line.

lessons.title: Following a failure through several functions

conceptCard.title: Following a failure through several functions
conceptCard.body: An error moves up the call stack through each caller until a catch handles it, and finally runs on the way. In a promise chain, a rejection skips then steps until a catch. A handler that swallows an error hides it from its callers.

items.prompt: A weather log stores three daily temperatures. The loop records the change from each day to the next. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. On the last pass temps[3] does not exist, so undefined - 5 is NaN, and push adds it.
You thought a read past the end adds nothing, so the result would be one value short. The loop runs three passes, and every pass pushes whatever the subtraction gives.
You thought reading an index past the end stops the program. An index with no item does not throw; the code simply keeps going with whatever that read gives.

items.explanation: Three temperatures have indexes 0 to 2. On the last pass temps[i + 1] is temps[3], which does not exist, so undefined - 5 is NaN and push adds it. The loop should stop one pass earlier.
hints: Look at line 5: which two indexes does it read on the last pass?
The last valid index is one less than the length, and i + 1 reaches one further.
Work out what the subtraction gives when its left value is missing.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Two slices of a queue are printed. Which statement explains why the first one has two items?

options.text: The end index is excluded, so slice(1, 3) takes the items at indexes 1 and 2.
options.feedback: Right. slice reads from the start index up to, but not including, the end index.

options.text: The end index is included, so slice(1, 3) should return three items and the output is wrong.
options.feedback: You counted the end index as part of the slice. The first printed array holds two items, which an inclusive end would not produce.

options.text: The second number counts items, so slice(1, 3) takes three items from index 1.
options.feedback: You read the second number as an item count, as if slice(1, 3) asked for three items. The first printed array holds two, so that reading does not match the output.

items.explanation: slice(start, end) copies from start up to, but not including, end, so the number of items is end minus start. A negative start counts back from the end of the array.
hints: Count the items in the first printed array.
Think about which of the two numbers is a position that is left out.
The length of a slice is end minus start.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Page 2 of the table should list rows 4, 5 and 6, but it prints a different slice. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. Pages count from 1, so page 2 starts after one full page of three rows.
That starts at index 5, which is the sixth row, so the slice shows the wrong rows.
That is one slot after the real start. Page 2 would begin at its second row instead of its first.

items.explanation: Page numbers start at 1 but indexes start at 0. Page 2 skips one full page, so its first index is (page - 1) * size. Using page * size skips two pages.
hints: Work out the index of row 4 and compare it with start.
Page 1 must start at index 0.
Count how many whole pages come before page 2.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write the body of chunk(list, n), with n at least 1. Group the items into arrays of n, in order; the last may hold fewer. An empty list gives [].
items.explanation: Start each page at i and step by n. slice(i, i + n) excludes its end, so it takes n items and stops safely at the end of the list. The loop must stop when i reaches the length.
hints: Think of one page per step of the loop.
slice excludes its end index and tolerates an end past the array.
One index that moves forward by a fixed amount can drive the whole loop; decide the step and when it stops.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A plant shop copies a shelf with spread, then edits the copy. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The copy has its own name, but its pots property points at the same array as the original.
You expected spread to duplicate everything inside shelf, so the push stays on the copy. Spread copies one level of properties, and what pots holds is a reference to an array.
You expected assigning copy.name to change shelf.name too, as if both names were one object. copy is a new object made on line 5, and name holds a text, not a reference.

items.explanation: Spread makes a shallow copy. The name text is copied, so changing it does not touch the original. The pots array is shared by reference, so push changes the original too.
hints: Compare what the two lines before the print change.
A shallow copy duplicates the top level only.
Ask for each property whether the copy holds its own value or the same one as the original.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A shop sorts its price list and keeps the result in a second name. Which statement explains the output?

options.text: sort reorders the array in place and returns that same array, so both names point to it.
options.feedback: Right. sort changes the array it is called on and gives back the same array.

options.text: sort returns a new sorted array and leaves prices in its original order.
options.feedback: You thought sort returns a new array and leaves prices in its original order. The line that prints prices runs after the sort call, and it shows the order after that call.

options.text: sort reorders prices but returns a separate copy, so the two names are different arrays.
options.feedback: You thought sort returns a copy, so sorted and prices are different arrays. The last line asks whether two names point at the same array, which depends on what sort returns.

items.explanation: Array sort is a mutating method: it reorders the array in place and returns a reference to the same array. To keep the original order, sort a copy.
hints: Look at what the first printed line shows about prices.
Some array methods change the array they are called on.
Compare the two names: are they two arrays or one?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The cart should keep its weights while doubled holds new ones, but both lists change. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The callback now builds a new object, so the original cart item is never changed.
This doubles the weight by writing into o, the original cart item. It still changes the original.
That is the same change written longer. It still edits the original object that the callback received.

items.explanation: map builds a new array, but its callback receives the same objects. Writing o.kg edits the original. Return a new object instead of changing the one received.
hints: Which object does o refer to on line 3?
map copies the array, not the objects inside it.
The change on line 3 must happen on an object that cart does not hold.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The bakery needs a sorted copy while the bin keeps its order. Fill the blank so the program prints 3 4.

options.feedback: Right. Spread makes a new array, so sort and push leave the bin alone.
entries() returns an iterator, not an array, and an iterator has no sort method, so the program throws a TypeError.
This is a second name for the same array, so push grows the bin too and the program prints 4 4.
reverse works in place and returns the same array, so the bin still grows with the push.
splice removes the items from the bin and returns them, so the bin ends up empty.

items.explanation: sort and push change the array they run on. To keep bin unchanged, sort a copy made with spread. A second name or a method that works in place does not make a copy.
hints: Look at which array push changes.
A copy is a new array, not another name for the bin.
Decide for each chip whether bin still has three items afterwards and whether out is a different array from bin.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A scoreboard value is read, then written back after an await. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. bump read 1 before its await, line 9 ran while it waited, and the write after the await stores 1 + 1 over the newer value.
You thought bump finished before line 9. The await hands control back to the caller, so line 9 runs before bump's last line.
You thought calling bump postpones its whole body until the caller finishes. The body up to its first await runs at once, so old is read on line 3 first.

items.explanation: bump reads old as 1, then the await hands control back, so line 9 sets pts to 10. When bump resumes it writes old + 1, which is 2, over the newer 10.
hints: Find which line reads pts into old and which line writes it back.
A value read before an await can be stale when the code continues after it.
Decide whether line 9 runs before or after line 5.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Two sales start at the same moment on a stock of 5. Which statement explains the printed 4?

options.text: Both calls read 5 before either writes, so the second write stores 4 again.
options.feedback: Right. Each call read a value that went stale during the await, and the last write replaced the first.

options.text: The second call is skipped while the first call is still waiting, so the stock goes down only once.
options.feedback: You treated the first call, still paused at its await, as a lock that stops the second one. Each call runs its own copy of the body, so a call in progress blocks nothing.

options.text: await makes each call finish before the next starts, so the stock should reach 3 but a bug skips one.
options.feedback: You thought await makes each call finish before the next starts. Nothing here waits for the first call; the second sell() starts while the first one is paused.

items.explanation: The first call reads 5 and pauses. The second call reads 5 too. Both resume and write 5 - 1, so one update is lost. Read the value after the await, or avoid keeping a stale copy.
hints: Follow the order of lines 3 and 5 for both calls.
A value saved before an await can be stale after it.
Compare what seen holds on line 5 with what qty holds by then.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The log should show the latte before served, but it shows only served. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. serve pauses until brew finishes, so the latte is added before served.
return ends serve at that line, so the lines that push served and print never run.
A timer only starts the brew later. serve does not wait for it, so the print runs before the latte is added.

items.explanation: Calling an async function starts it and returns a promise. Without await, serve carries on at once, and brew adds the cup after the print. Awaiting the promise keeps the steps in order.
hints: Line 7 starts brew; what makes serve wait for it?
An async call returns a promise that serve must wait on.
Only line 7 needs to change; the new line still starts brew with "latte".
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Write interleave(jobs): each job is [name, steps], at least one step. Jobs take turns, one step each, like awaiting calls. Return the steps in order, like 'a1'.
items.explanation: Keep the jobs in a queue. Take the first job, count one more step for it and record name plus step number. If it has steps left, put it at the back, so the jobs take turns.
hints: Keep the jobs in a line and take them from the front.
After a job runs one step it goes to the back of the line, unless it has no steps left.
A loop that runs while jobs remain can handle one step per turn; decide where a job goes after its step.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: An oven error travels up through two callers. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The throw skips the rest of prep's try block, finally still runs, and the outer catch gets the error.
You thought the push of a still runs after bake throws. A throw leaves the function at once, so the statements after the throwing call in that try block do not run.
You thought finally is skipped while an error passes through. A finally block belongs to its try, and it runs whether that try ends normally or by a throw.

items.explanation: The throw leaves bake and skips the rest of prep's try block. finally runs on the way out, then the error reaches the catch in the caller, which logs its name.
hints: Follow the error out of bake, one caller at a time.
A throw skips the rest of its block, but finally still runs.
Decide which pushes still run after the throw, and which block always runs on the way out.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A failure starts in read and passes through two more functions. Which statement explains the printed line?

options.text: The catch in parse handles the failure and returns 0, so load and the caller receive a normal value.
options.feedback: Right. A failure ends at the first handler that deals with it; the functions above it see a normal result.

options.text: The rejection passes through parse and load to the final catch, which prints its name.
options.feedback: You thought the chain stays rejected after parse's catch. Ask what promise parse returns once its catch handler has run.

options.text: The catch handler's result is thrown away, so load adds 1 to undefined and prints NaN.
options.feedback: You thought a catch handler's return value is discarded. Look at line 4: the handler returns 0, and the promise it creates carries that value.

items.explanation: A failure travels up only until a handler deals with it. The catch in parse returns 0, which fulfils the promise parse gives back, so load adds 1 and the last then prints 1. The final catch never runs.
hints: Follow the failure from line 2 up through parse and load, one function at a time.
A catch that returns normally ends the failure for the callers above it.
Decide what the promise returned by parse holds after line 4 has run.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The caller should print TypeError, but the inner function hides the failure. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. The error is passed on, so the outer catch sees it and prints its name.
The error becomes an ordinary return value. No error reaches the outer catch, so nothing is printed.
This reports the failure here, but it ends in this function and the outer catch never runs.

items.explanation: A catch that returns a value handles the error and ends the failure there. Callers never learn of it. To let a caller decide, rethrow the error from the catch.
hints: Follow line 2's error: who gets it first?
A catch ends the failure unless it throws again.
The inner catch has to do something with e so that the outer try can see it.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A loader starts rejected and the caller should recover from it. Fill the two blanks so the program prints ['B'].

options.feedback: Right. The chain starts rejected, so step A is skipped.
Right. It runs for the rejection, and the chain is fulfilled after it.
The loader would give a fulfilled promise, so A is pushed and the recovery step is skipped, which prints ['A'].
A success step is skipped for a rejection, so the rejection stays unhandled and the log is never printed.
finally runs but passes the rejection on, so the last step is skipped and the log is never printed.

items.explanation: A rejected promise skips success steps all the way out of load and run. Only a step made for failures runs, and after it the chain is fulfilled again, so the last step prints.
hints: Follow the promise from load through run, step by step, with each choice.
Decide how the promise starts, then which step may react to it.
The second blank must run for a failure and let the chain continue.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author
